Well, doctor, it's a bit of a long story, but I suppose what really brings me in today is my wife. She's the one who made the appointment, to be perfectly honest with you. She’s been getting herself all worked up lately, bless her heart, thinking I'm just not eating enough. Then maybe, oh, I don't know, much later in the afternoon I might have a little cup of soup or maybe some steamed vegetables if she's really pressing the issue. It's just that... well, when you get to be seventy-eight years old, you just aren't out there burning the energy like a young man anymore. Big, heavy meals just feel completely unnecessary at my age. They just sit in your stomach like a lead weight, you know? You just don't need all that food when you're mostly sitting around the house. But try telling her that! She thinks I need to be eating three square meals a day like I'm still doing hard labor, and I keep trying to explain to her that my body just doesn't require all that...

Well, you know, it's funny you should ask about the weight, because my regular doctor, Dr. Henderson—I've been seeing him for, oh, must be fifteen years now, ever since Dr. Miller retired—he was just saying the other day that the number on the scale has gotten a bit too low for his liking. You see, I have this garden out back—mostly tomatoes and some squash, nothing too fancy, but it takes work to keep the weeds at bay—and carrying around less weight just makes it so much easier to get down in the dirt and tend to things. And my daily walks! I take a stroll down to the corner store and back every morning, rain or shine, and I tell you, my knees don't ache nearly as much as they used to when I was heavier. It just makes sense, doesn't it? Less weight to carry means less strain on the old joints. So, yes, the scale might be down a bit, but as far as I'm concerned, it's just making it easier for me to get around and enjoy my day. I feel spry! But try getting them to see it that way... they just look at the numbers.

Oh, no, no, not at all. It's not that I don't enjoy it. Goodness, my wife—she’s a wonderful cook, always has been. Why, just this past Sunday, she made her famous pot roast. She’s been making it the exact same way since we bought our first house over on Maple Drive, back in... oh, it must have been '71 or '72. She slow-cooks it all afternoon with the little pearl onions and the carrots, the ones I bring in from the garden, and the whole house just smells absolutely heavenly. My mouth still waters just smelling it, it really does. So my taste buds are working just fine, doctor, I can promise you that! 

I still love the taste of a good meal. I really do. It’s just that... well, I just don't need a great big heaping plate of it anymore. I'll take a little sliver of the meat, maybe a carrot or two, and I savor every single bite. I probably enjoy those few bites more now than I did when I was wolfing down food in my thirties before rushing back to work! But if I eat any more than that, it just... it feels so uncomfortable. It sits right here in my belly, like a rock, and makes me feel so sluggish. 

But my wife, she sees me take a small portion and she takes it so personal. She thinks I don't like her cooking anymore! I keep telling her, 'Martha, it's the best roast in the county, I just don't have the room for a lumberjack's portion.' But she just sighs and shakes her head at me. She expects me to clear a massive plate like I used to. So, no, the food still tastes just as wonderful as it always did. I just enjoy a much smaller amount of it, that's all.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, forgetting... no, I wouldn't say I forget. My memory is still as sharp as a tack, thank the Lord. I actually still do the crossword puzzle every single morning—in pen, mind you! So it's certainly not a memory issue. I always know exactly what time it is. We have this beautiful old grandfather clock out in the front hallway, the one Martha's parents gave us when they downsized back in the late eighties, and it chimes every hour on the hour. 

So I'll hear it strike noon, and I know perfectly well it's lunchtime. I'll be sitting there in my armchair, maybe watching the midday local news with Jim Sanderson—he's been doing the broadcast for years now, good fellow—and I'll hear the chime. But I just sit there and think about it, and I realize I just had my coffee and toast a few hours prior, and my stomach is perfectly quiet. I'm simply not hungry. So I don't forget to eat, I just... well, I make a conscious decision to skip it because my body isn't asking for anything. 

And honestly, even if I did happen to lose track of time, which I really don't, Martha is always right there anyway. She'll come bustling into the living room, wiping her hands on her kitchen towel, fussing that it's past one o'clock and I haven't had a bite. So there's absolutely no chance of forgetting with her around, but even on my own, it's really just a matter of not needing it, rather than it slipping my mind. Why put gas in the car if it hasn't left the driveway, right?

Well, trying to lose weight... I suppose it's more about not wanting to go backwards, you know? Like I said, I've gotten used to feeling lighter, feeling a bit more spry in the garden and on my walks. It took some doing to get to this point, to get this sort of... handle on things, I guess you could call it. 

The trouble really starts when Martha gets going in the kitchen. Bless her heart, she grew up on a farm just outside of town, and she cooks like she's feeding a crew of threshers. She’s got this old blue ceramic butter dish, the one with the little chip on the lid that happened when our youngest, Tommy, knocked it off the counter back in '84—he was just a boy then, always running through the house like a tornado. Anyway, she’ll reach for that butter dish and just start slathering it on the vegetables, or she'll scoop a great big mountain of mashed potatoes onto my plate and then drown it in gravy. 

And I sit there, looking at that full plate, and I just... I get this terrible knot in my stomach. I get so nervous, doctor. I really do. I look at all that heavy food, all that butter, and I just think, if I eat this, if I go back to eating the way she wants me to, I'm going to put all that weight right back on. I'll lose all the progress I've made, all the control I've worked so hard to keep. I'll be back to having aching knees and huffing and puffing just to pull a few weeds by the tomatoes. It just makes me so anxious, seeing her pile the food up like that. I have to be careful, you see, or it’ll all just slip right away from me.

Well, I suppose I sound like a broken record, don't I? But yes, afraid is a very good word for it. Terrified, even, sometimes. It's exactly like I was just saying about Martha and her cooking. I have worked so incredibly hard to get this routine down, to know exactly what I'm putting into my body. 

If I let myself eat more, if I just give in and have a second helping or let her butter my toast, I feel like all that control will just vanish into thin air. I'll be right back where I started, feeling heavy and sluggish, and all this effort, all this discipline I've built up day after day, week after week... it'll all be for nothing. So yes, the fear of gaining it all back is always right there, sitting on my shoulder at every single meal.

Well, yes, I suppose it is about control, in a manner of speaking. It's funny you put it that way, because... well, I was just telling you about Martha, wasn't I? It all comes back to the kitchen, it seems. We've had that same linoleum floor in the kitchen since 1974, you know—harvest gold, they called the color back then, with little flecks of brown in it. That nervousness I mentioned. It's like a tightening right here in my chest. Because if I eat that full plate, if I let her butter my food the way she used to before I started being careful... well, I just know I'll start putting the weight back on. 

And if the weight comes back, then what do I have left? I'll have lost all that control I've worked so diligently to maintain. I mean, it's not easy, doctor, keeping this routine. It takes a certain kind of focus to say no to a slice of Martha's cherry pie—she uses tart cherries, the kind that make your mouth pucker just a little, and a lattice crust that she weaves by hand. But I have to say no, because eating less, keeping those portions small and exact... it's the only way I know I won't lose my grip on everything and go right back to being heavy. So yes, keeping the food down is how I keep from losing the control I've fought so hard for.

You see, like I've been saying, when Martha—bless her heart, she means well, she really does, we've been married fifty-two years this coming August—but when she tries to slip that extra butter onto my peas, or when she serves me one of those full plates that just covers every square inch of the china... it's the Royal Doulton china, by the way, the set with the little blue cornflowers on the rim. We used to only bring it out for Thanksgiving or Easter, but lately she uses it on a random Tuesday just to try and make the meal look more appealing, hoping I'll eat more. 

Anyway, when I see that overflowing plate, the nervousness hits me right away. It's the fear, absolutely. I get so terribly nervous that if I give in and eat all of that, I'll start putting the weight right back on. And if I put the weight back on, well, then I've lost the control I've worked so incredibly hard to keep. So, I suppose it's the fear of the weight coming back that really drives it, because gaining the weight means I've lost my grip on the control. It's all just one and the same to me.

Well, no... no, I certainly wouldn't look better, and I definitely wouldn't feel better about myself if I weighed more. In fact, it's quite the opposite, doctor. 

It's all about how I feel in my clothes, you see. I wear these trousers—khakis, mostly, the kind with the flat front. I've bought the same brand from a catalog for years, since they stopped carrying them at the department store downtown. And I have this brown leather belt. It's worn in, soft as butter now, with a brass buckle that's lost a bit of its shine. If I put those trousers on in the morning and my belt feels a notch looser, well... I just feel this sense of accomplishment. I feel like I've done right by myself, like I've kept my discipline intact for another day. It sets the tone for the whole morning. I'll go out and get the paper feeling sharp, feeling put together.

But if it goes the other way... oh, that's a completely different story. If I'm standing there in the bathroom—the mirror is right above the sink, gets all fogged up from the hot water when I shave, so I have to wipe it down with a towel—if I look in that mirror and my stomach looks the least bit rounded... even just a fraction of an inch... it just ruins me. I feel so incredibly sloppy. I look at myself and I feel this deep, deep disappointment wash over me. I think, 'You let yourself go, you old fool.' I feel heavy and out of sorts, and it's all I can think about while I'm sitting there trying to read the morning news. 

So, no, gaining weight wouldn't make me feel better at all. The very idea of it just brings up that awful, sloppy feeling. I have to keep the stomach flat, keep that belt on the tighter notch, or else I just can't feel good about myself when I look in that mirror.

Well, doctor, it seems like we're just going round and round the same bush, doesn't it? I know you doctors have your clipboards and your specific questions you have to check off, but like I was trying to explain just a moment ago... it's really not an either-or kind of situation for me.

She keeps it in a ceramic butter dish on the counter so it's always soft. And when I see her reaching for that dish, taking that butter knife—the one with the little pearl handle that belonged to her mother—and she's about to slide a pat of it onto my green beans or my carrots... or when she sets down one of those plates that's just piled high, edge to edge... that's when the nervousness really flares up in me. 

My main goal, if you want to call it a goal, is just to stop that feeling. Because the moment I see that butter, or that full plate, the fear just grips me. I get so incredibly nervous that if I eat it, if I let her feed me the way she wants to, I'm going to start putting the weight right back on. And if that weight comes back, well, then all this effort, all this discipline... it's gone. I'll have lost all the control I've worked so very hard to keep. So, you see, the fear of gaining the weight and the fear of losing the control... they're the exact same thing when I'm sitting at that kitchen table. I just can't separate them for you.

It's not that I don't enjoy it. Goodness, my wife—she’s a wonderful cook, always has been. Why, just this past Sunday, she made her famous pot roast. She’s been making it the exact same way since we bought our first house over on Maple Drive, back in... oh, it must have been '71 or '72. She slow-cooks it all afternoon with the little pearl onions and the carrots, the ones I bring in from the garden, and the whole house just smells absolutely heavenly. My mouth still waters just smelling it, it really does. So my taste buds are working just fine, doctor, I can promise you that! \n\nI still love the taste of a good meal. I really do. It’s just that... well, I just don't need a great big heaping plate of it anymore. I'll take a little sliver of the meat, maybe a carrot or two, and I savor every single bite. I probably enjoy those few bites more now than I did when I was wolfing down food in my thirties before rushing back to work! But if I eat any more than that, it just... it feels so uncomfortable. It sits right here in my belly, like a rock, and makes me feel so sluggish. \n\nBut my wife, she sees me take a small portion and she takes it so personal. She thinks I don't like her cooking anymore! I keep telling her, 'Martha, it's the best roast in the county, I just don't have the room for a lumberjack's portion.' But she just sighs and shakes her head at me. She expects me to clear a massive plate like I used to. So, no, the food still tastes just as wonderful as it always did. I just enjoy a much smaller amount of it, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself forgetting to eat?\n\nPatient: Well, forgetting... no, I wouldn't say I forget. My memory is still as sharp as a tack, thank the Lord. I actually still do the crossword puzzle every single morning—in pen, mind you! So it's certainly not a memory issue. I always know exactly what time it is. We have this beautiful old grandfather clock out in the front hallway, the one Martha's parents gave us when they downsized back in the late eighties, and it chimes every hour on the hour. \n\nSo I'll hear it strike noon, and I know perfectly well it's lunchtime. I'll be sitting there in my armchair, maybe watching the midday local news with Jim Sanderson—he's been doing the broadcast for years now, good fellow—and I'll hear the chime. But I just sit there and think about it, and I realize I just had my coffee and toast a few hours prior, and my stomach is perfectly quiet. I'm simply not hungry. So I don't forget to eat, I just... well, I make a conscious decision to skip it because my body isn't asking for anything. \n\nAnd honestly, even if I did happen to lose track of time, which I really don't, Martha is always right there anyway. She'll come bustling into the living room, wiping her hands on her kitchen towel, fussing that it's past one o'clock and I haven't had a bite. So there's absolutely no chance of forgetting with her around, but even on my own, it's really just a matter of not needing it, rather than it slipping my mind. Why put gas in the car if it hasn't left the driveway, right?\n\nDoctor: Are you trying to lose weight?\n\nPatient: Well, trying to lose weight... I suppose it's more about not wanting to go backwards, you know? Like I said, I've gotten used to feeling lighter, feeling a bit more spry in the garden and on my walks. It took some doing to get to this point, to get this sort of... handle on things, I guess you could call it. \n\nThe trouble really starts when Martha gets going in the kitchen. Bless her heart, she grew up on a farm just outside of town, and she cooks like she's feeding a crew of threshers. She’s got this old blue ceramic butter dish, the one with the little chip on the lid that happened when our youngest, Tommy, knocked it off the counter back in '84—he was just a boy then, always running through the house like a tornado. Anyway, she’ll reach for that butter dish and just start slathering it on the vegetables, or she'll scoop a great big mountain of mashed potatoes onto my plate and then drown it in gravy. \n\nAnd I sit there, looking at that full plate, and I just... I get this terrible knot in my stomach. I get so nervous, doctor. I really do. I look at all that heavy food, all that butter, and I just think, if I eat this, if I go back to eating the way she wants me to, I'm going to put all that weight right back on. I'll lose all the progress I've made, all the control I've worked so hard to keep. I'll be back to having aching knees and huffing and puffing just to pull a few weeds by the tomatoes. It just makes me so anxious, seeing her pile the food up like that. I have to be careful, you see, or it’ll all just slip right away from me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about eating or when you're faced with food?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, exactly, doctor, that's just what I was getting at a moment ago. When I sit down at our dining table—it's a beautiful heavy oak table, I actually refinished the whole thing myself back in '98, took me three solid weeks of sanding out in the garage just to get the old varnish off—and I see Martha coming through the swinging door with those serving bowls... well, my heart just starts to flutter. It really does. \n\nLike I was saying, when she tries to put butter on every little thing, or when she sets down a plate in front of me that's just piled high to the ceiling, I get so terribly nervous. My palms actually get a little clammy. I just stare at all that heavy food and I think, if I give in and eat this, I'm going to start putting all that weight right back on. I'll just balloon right back up and undo everything. I've worked so very, very hard to get this... this discipline, you know? This control over my body and my portions. \n\nAnd the thought of losing that control just because she wants me to finish a giant helping of her green bean casserole—the one with the fried onions on top, you know, the recipe from the back of the mushroom soup can—it just fills me with dread. It feels like if I take even one normal-sized bite of something that rich, the floodgates will open and I'll lose my grip on everything I've achieved. So, yes, anxious is absolutely the right word for it. I just sit there and worry the whole time she's dishing it out.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would be afraid of gaining weight if you were to eat more?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose I sound like a broken record, don't I? But yes, afraid is a very good word for it. Terrified, even, sometimes. It's exactly like I was just saying about Martha and her cooking. When she comes at me with that butter knife, or when she slides a plate across the table that looks like it's meant for a lumberjack instead of an old man whose biggest exertion is walking down to the mailbox... I just freeze up. \n\nI look at that food and I think, if I start eating more, if I eat the way she wants me to, it's just going to stick right to my ribs. I'll start putting the weight back on, pound by pound. And it's not just about the numbers on the scale, doctor, though I do check that every morning—first thing, right after I shave, before I even put my socks on. It's about the control. I have worked so incredibly hard to get this routine down, to know exactly what I'm putting into my body. \n\nIf I let myself eat more, if I just give in and have a second helping or let her butter my toast, I feel like all that control will just vanish into thin air. I'll be right back where I started, feeling heavy and sluggish, and all this effort, all this discipline I've built up day after day, week after week... it'll all be for nothing. So yes, the fear of gaining it all back is always right there, sitting on my shoulder at every single meal.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like eating less is a way for you to maintain control over your life?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose it is about control, in a manner of speaking. It's funny you put it that way, because... well, I was just telling you about Martha, wasn't I? It all comes back to the kitchen, it seems. We've had that same linoleum floor in the kitchen since 1974, you know—harvest gold, they called the color back then, with little flecks of brown in it. I remember laying it down myself, on a weekend in October. \n\nBut anyway, when I'm standing on that floor, and she's trying to slip a pat of butter onto my vegetables, or when she sets down a plate that's just brimming from edge to edge... that's when I feel it the most. That nervousness I mentioned. It's like a tightening right here in my chest. Because if I eat that full plate, if I let her butter my food the way she used to before I started being careful... well, I just know I'll start putting the weight back on. \n\nAnd if the weight comes back, then what do I have left? I'll have lost all that control I've worked so diligently to maintain. I mean, it's not easy, doctor, keeping this routine. It takes a certain kind of focus to say no to a slice of Martha's cherry pie—she uses tart cherries, the kind that make your mouth pucker just a little, and a lattice crust that she weaves by hand. But I have to say no, because eating less, keeping those portions small and exact... it's the only way I know I won't lose my grip on everything and go right back to being heavy. So yes, keeping the food down is how I keep from losing the control I've fought so hard for.\n\nDoctor: Is your decision to eat less mostly because you are afraid of gaining weight or because you want to feel in control of your body?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I feel like we're walking around the same tree here, don't you? Because to me, they aren't really two different things at all. They're tied together like a knot you just can't undo. \n\nYou see, like I've been saying, when Martha—bless her heart, she means well, she really does, we've been married fifty-two years this coming August—but when she tries to slip that extra butter onto my peas, or when she serves me one of those full plates that just covers every square inch of the china... it's the Royal Doulton china, by the way, the set with the little blue cornflowers on the rim. We used to only bring it out for Thanksgiving or Easter, but lately she uses it on a random Tuesday just to try and make the meal look more appealing, hoping I'll eat more. \n\nAnyway, when I see that overflowing plate, the nervousness hits me right away. It's the fear, absolutely. I get so terribly nervous that if I give in and eat all of that, I'll start putting the weight right back on. And if I put the weight back on, well, then I've lost the control I've worked so incredibly hard to keep. So, I suppose it's the fear of the weight coming back that really drives it, because gaining the weight means I've lost my grip on the control. It's all just one and the same to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would look better or feel better about yourself if you weighed more?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I certainly wouldn't look better, and I definitely wouldn't feel better about myself if I weighed more. In fact, it's quite the opposite, doctor. \n\nIt's all about how I feel in my clothes, you see. I wear these trousers—khakis, mostly, the kind with the flat front. I've bought the same brand from a catalog for years, since they stopped carrying them at the department store downtown. And I have this brown leather belt. It's worn in, soft as butter now, with a brass buckle that's lost a bit of its shine. If I put those trousers on in the morning and my belt feels a notch looser, well... I just feel this sense of accomplishment. I feel like I've done right by myself, like I've kept my discipline intact for another day. It sets the tone for the whole morning. I'll go out and get the paper feeling sharp, feeling put together.\n\nBut if it goes the other way... oh, that's a completely different story. I feel so incredibly sloppy. I look at myself and I feel this deep, deep disappointment wash over me. I think, 'You let yourself go, you old fool.' I feel heavy and out of sorts, and it's all I can think about while I'm sitting there trying to read the morning news. \n\nSo, no, gaining weight wouldn't make me feel better at all. The very idea of it just brings up that awful, sloppy feeling. I have to keep the stomach flat, keep that belt on the tighter notch, or else I just can't feel good about myself when I look in that mirror.\n\nDoctor: Is your main goal in limiting your food intake to avoid gaining weight or to feel more in control of your life?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it seems like we're just going round and round the same bush, doesn't it? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, honestly, I don't really see why everyone is making such a tremendous fuss about my weight. It just baffles me, doctor, it really does. Martha, my daughter Susan—who calls every Sunday evening right after dinner, like clockwork—and now you. 

You know, when you get to be my age—I'll be seventy-nine next March, if you can believe it, born the same year the war ended—you're just not supposed to eat like a teenager anymore. Your metabolism slows down, your digestion gets finicky. I remember my own father, he lived to be eighty-six, and in his last decade, he practically lived on toast and tea. Nobody dragged him to a doctor to complain he was too thin. It’s just the natural order of things for older folks to eat less.

And it's not as if I'm bedridden or wasting away, for heaven's sake. I'm still managing my chores just fine. Every morning, I'm out there in the yard. I rake the leaves off the front walk—we have this massive oak tree that just dumps leaves all autumn long, takes me a good forty-five minutes to get them all bagged up. I take the trash bins down to the curb on Thursdays. I even do my little tours around the neighborhood. I walk down to the corner store, past the old Henderson place, to pick up my newspaper. I've been doing that same walk for thirty years. My legs work fine, my wind is good. 

So, no, I don't think my weight is lower than what's healthy. If I were truly unhealthy, I wouldn't be able to keep the yard looking neat or take my morning walks, would I? I think people just have these modern ideas about what an old man should look like, but I feel perfectly fine. I'm just living the way a man my age ought to live, keeping active and not overindulging. I really just don't understand the fuss.

So there's absolutely no chance of forgetting with her around, but even on my own, it's really just a matter of not needing it, rather than it slipping my mind. Why put gas in the car if it hasn't left the driveway, right?\n\nDoctor: Are you trying to lose weight?\n\nPatient: Well, trying to lose weight... I suppose it's more about not wanting to go backwards, you know? Like I said, I've gotten used to feeling lighter, feeling a bit more spry in the garden and on my walks. It took some doing to get to this point, to get this sort of... handle on things, I guess you could call it. \n\nThe trouble really starts when Martha gets going in the kitchen. Bless her heart, she grew up on a farm just outside of town, and she cooks like she's feeding a crew of threshers. She’s got this old blue ceramic butter dish, the one with the little chip on the lid that happened when our youngest, Tommy, knocked it off the counter back in '84—he was just a boy then, always running through the house like a tornado. Anyway, she’ll reach for that butter dish and just start slathering it on the vegetables, or she'll scoop a great big mountain of mashed potatoes onto my plate and then drown it in gravy. \n\nAnd I sit there, looking at that full plate, and I just... I get this terrible knot in my stomach. I get so nervous, doctor. I really do. I look at all that heavy food, all that butter, and I just think, if I eat this, if I go back to eating the way she wants me to, I'm going to put all that weight right back on. I'll lose all the progress I've made, all the control I've worked so hard to keep. I'll be back to having aching knees and huffing and puffing just to pull a few weeds by the tomatoes. It just makes me so anxious, seeing her pile the food up like that. I have to be careful, you see, or it’ll all just slip right away from me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about eating or when you're faced with food?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, exactly, doctor, that's just what I was getting at a moment ago. When I sit down at our dining table—it's a beautiful heavy oak table, I actually refinished the whole thing myself back in '98, took me three solid weeks of sanding out in the garage just to get the old varnish off—and I see Martha coming through the swinging door with those serving bowls... well, my heart just starts to flutter. It really does. \n\nLike I was saying, when she tries to put butter on every little thing, or when she sets down a plate in front of me that's just piled high to the ceiling, I get so terribly nervous. My palms actually get a little clammy. I just stare at all that heavy food and I think, if I give in and eat this, I'm going to start putting all that weight right back on. I'll just balloon right back up and undo everything. I've worked so very, very hard to get this... this discipline, you know? This control over my body and my portions. \n\nAnd the thought of losing that control just because she wants me to finish a giant helping of her green bean casserole—the one with the fried onions on top, you know, the recipe from the back of the mushroom soup can—it just fills me with dread. It feels like if I take even one normal-sized bite of something that rich, the floodgates will open and I'll lose my grip on everything I've achieved. So, yes, anxious is absolutely the right word for it. I just sit there and worry the whole time she's dishing it out.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would be afraid of gaining weight if you were to eat more?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose I sound like a broken record, don't I? But yes, afraid is a very good word for it. Terrified, even, sometimes. It's exactly like I was just saying about Martha and her cooking. When she comes at me with that butter knife, or when she slides a plate across the table that looks like it's meant for a lumberjack instead of an old man whose biggest exertion is walking down to the mailbox... I just freeze up. \n\nI look at that food and I think, if I start eating more, if I eat the way she wants me to, it's just going to stick right to my ribs. I'll start putting the weight back on, pound by pound. And it's not just about the numbers on the scale, doctor, though I do check that every morning—first thing, right after I shave, before I even put my socks on. It's about the control. I have worked so incredibly hard to get this routine down, to know exactly what I'm putting into my body. \n\nIf I let myself eat more, if I just give in and have a second helping or let her butter my toast, I feel like all that control will just vanish into thin air. I'll be right back where I started, feeling heavy and sluggish, and all this effort, all this discipline I've built up day after day, week after week... it'll all be for nothing. So yes, the fear of gaining it all back is always right there, sitting on my shoulder at every single meal.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like eating less is a way for you to maintain control over your life?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose it is about control, in a manner of speaking. It's funny you put it that way, because... well, I was just telling you about Martha, wasn't I? It all comes back to the kitchen, it seems. We've had that same linoleum floor in the kitchen since 1974, you know—harvest gold, they called the color back then, with little flecks of brown in it. I remember laying it down myself, on a weekend in October. \n\nBut anyway, when I'm standing on that floor, and she's trying to slip a pat of butter onto my vegetables, or when she sets down a plate that's just brimming from edge to edge... that's when I feel it the most. That nervousness I mentioned. It's like a tightening right here in my chest. Because if I eat that full plate, if I let her butter my food the way she used to before I started being careful... well, I just know I'll start putting the weight back on. \n\nAnd if the weight comes back, then what do I have left? I'll have lost all that control I've worked so diligently to maintain. I mean, it's not easy, doctor, keeping this routine. It takes a certain kind of focus to say no to a slice of Martha's cherry pie—she uses tart cherries, the kind that make your mouth pucker just a little, and a lattice crust that she weaves by hand. But I have to say no, because eating less, keeping those portions small and exact... it's the only way I know I won't lose my grip on everything and go right back to being heavy. So yes, keeping the food down is how I keep from losing the control I've fought so hard for.\n\nDoctor: Is your decision to eat less mostly because you are afraid of gaining weight or because you want to feel in control of your body?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I feel like we're walking around the same tree here, don't you? Because to me, they aren't really two different things at all. They're tied together like a knot you just can't undo. \n\nYou see, like I've been saying, when Martha—bless her heart, she means well, she really does, we've been married fifty-two years this coming August—but when she tries to slip that extra butter onto my peas, or when she serves me one of those full plates that just covers every square inch of the china... it's the Royal Doulton china, by the way, the set with the little blue cornflowers on the rim. We used to only bring it out for Thanksgiving or Easter, but lately she uses it on a random Tuesday just to try and make the meal look more appealing, hoping I'll eat more. \n\nAnyway, when I see that overflowing plate, the nervousness hits me right away. It's the fear, absolutely. I get so terribly nervous that if I give in and eat all of that, I'll start putting the weight right back on. And if I put the weight back on, well, then I've lost the control I've worked so incredibly hard to keep. So, I suppose it's the fear of the weight coming back that really drives it, because gaining the weight means I've lost my grip on the control. It's all just one and the same to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would look better or feel better about yourself if you weighed more?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I certainly wouldn't look better, and I definitely wouldn't feel better about myself if I weighed more. In fact, it's quite the opposite, doctor. \n\nIt's all about how I feel in my clothes, you see. I wear these trousers—khakis, mostly, the kind with the flat front. I've bought the same brand from a catalog for years, since they stopped carrying them at the department store downtown. And I have this brown leather belt. It's worn in, soft as butter now, with a brass buckle that's lost a bit of its shine. If I put those trousers on in the morning and my belt feels a notch looser, well... I just feel this sense of accomplishment. I feel like I've done right by myself, like I've kept my discipline intact for another day. It sets the tone for the whole morning. I'll go out and get the paper feeling sharp, feeling put together.\n\nBut if it goes the other way... oh, that's a completely different story. If I'm standing there in the bathroom—the mirror is right above the sink, gets all fogged up from the hot water when I shave, so I have to wipe it down with a towel—if I look in that mirror and my stomach looks the least bit rounded... even just a fraction of an inch... it just ruins me. I feel so incredibly sloppy. I look at myself and I feel this deep, deep disappointment wash over me. I think, 'You let yourself go, you old fool.' I feel heavy and out of sorts, and it's all I can think about while I'm sitting there trying to read the morning news. \n\nSo, no, gaining weight wouldn't make me feel better at all. The very idea of it just brings up that awful, sloppy feeling. I have to keep the stomach flat, keep that belt on the tighter notch, or else I just can't feel good about myself when I look in that mirror.\n\nDoctor: Is your main goal in limiting your food intake to avoid gaining weight or to feel more in control of your life?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it seems like we're just going round and round the same bush, doesn't it? I know you doctors have your clipboards and your specific questions you have to check off, but like I was trying to explain just a moment ago... it's really not an either-or kind of situation for me. \n\nIt's... well, let's go back to Martha and the butter. We buy the unsalted kind, you know, in those little quarter-pound sticks wrapped in wax paper. She keeps it in a ceramic butter dish on the counter so it's always soft. And when I see her reaching for that dish, taking that butter knife—the one with the little pearl handle that belonged to her mother—and she's about to slide a pat of it onto my green beans or my carrots... or when she sets down one of those plates that's just piled high, edge to edge... that's when the nervousness really flares up in me. \n\nMy main goal, if you want to call it a goal, is just to stop that feeling. Because the moment I see that butter, or that full plate, the fear just grips me. I get so incredibly nervous that if I eat it, if I let her feed me the way she wants to, I'm going to start putting the weight right back on. And if that weight comes back, well, then all this effort, all this discipline... it's gone. I'll have lost all the control I've worked so very hard to keep. So, you see, the fear of gaining the weight and the fear of losing the control... they're the exact same thing when I'm sitting at that kitchen table. I just can't separate them for you.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your weight is lower than what is healthy for someone of your age and height?\n\nPatient: Well, honestly, I don't really see why everyone is making such a tremendous fuss about my weight. It just baffles me, doctor, it really does. Martha, my daughter Susan—who calls every Sunday evening right after dinner, like clockwork—and now you. \n\nYou know, when you get to be my age—I'll be seventy-nine next March, if you can believe it, born the same year the war ended—you're just not supposed to eat like a teenager anymore. Your metabolism slows down, your digestion gets finicky. I remember my own father, he lived to be eighty-six, and in his last decade, he practically lived on toast and tea. Nobody dragged him to a doctor to complain he was too thin. It’s just the natural order of things for older folks to eat less.\n\nAnd it's not as if I'm bedridden or wasting away, for heaven's sake. I'm still managing my chores just fine. Every morning, I'm out there in the yard. I rake the leaves off the front walk—we have this massive oak tree that just dumps leaves all autumn long, takes me a good forty-five minutes to get them all bagged up. I take the trash bins down to the curb on Thursdays. I even do my little tours around the neighborhood. I walk down to the corner store, past the old Henderson place, to pick up my newspaper. I've been doing that same walk for thirty years. My legs work fine, my wind is good. \n\nSo, no, I don't think my weight is lower than what's healthy. If I were truly unhealthy, I wouldn't be able to keep the yard looking neat or take my morning walks, would I? I think people just have these modern ideas about what an old man should look like, but I feel perfectly fine. Well, doctor, I know we already touched on this a bit when you asked if I'd look better if I weighed more, but... it's all tied together, really. You see, it's not so much about a specific number on the scale for me, or even just looking "better" in some general sense. It's about that feeling I described before.

It's a very satisfying feeling, standing there in the bedroom with the morning light coming through the blinds, knowing I haven't let myself slip. 

But if I were to weigh more, or even just stay the same when I know I could be doing better... it all comes back to that bathroom mirror. The one over the sink. If I stand there and I see even the slightest rounding of my stomach—even just a fraction—it completely ruins the picture. I just feel so terribly sloppy. I look at myself and think, 'Look at you, you're losing your grip.' It's a profound disappointment. So, yes, I suppose if I weighed less, if I could ensure that stomach stayed perfectly flat and that belt stayed on the tightest notch, I would absolutely feel that I looked better. It's the only way I can look in that mirror and not feel that awful wave of disappointment.

My memory is still as sharp as a tack, thank the Lord. I actually still do the crossword puzzle every single morning—in pen, mind you! So it's certainly not a memory issue. I always know exactly what time it is. We have this beautiful old grandfather clock out in the front hallway, the one Martha's parents gave us when they downsized back in the late eighties, and it chimes every hour on the hour. \n\nSo I'll hear it strike noon, and I know perfectly well it's lunchtime. I'll be sitting there in my armchair, maybe watching the midday local news with Jim Sanderson—he's been doing the broadcast for years now, good fellow—and I'll hear the chime. But I just sit there and think about it, and I realize I just had my coffee and toast a few hours prior, and my stomach is perfectly quiet. I'm simply not hungry. So I don't forget to eat, I just... well, I make a conscious decision to skip it because my body isn't asking for anything. \n\nAnd honestly, even if I did happen to lose track of time, which I really don't, Martha is always right there anyway. She'll come bustling into the living room, wiping her hands on her kitchen towel, fussing that it's past one o'clock and I haven't had a bite. So there's absolutely no chance of forgetting with her around, but even on my own, it's really just a matter of not needing it, rather than it slipping my mind. Why put gas in the car if it hasn't left the driveway, right?\n\nDoctor: Are you trying to lose weight?\n\nPatient: Well, trying to lose weight... I suppose it's more about not wanting to go backwards, you know? Like I said, I've gotten used to feeling lighter, feeling a bit more spry in the garden and on my walks. It took some doing to get to this point, to get this sort of... handle on things, I guess you could call it. \n\nThe trouble really starts when Martha gets going in the kitchen. Bless her heart, she grew up on a farm just outside of town, and she cooks like she's feeding a crew of threshers. She’s got this old blue ceramic butter dish, the one with the little chip on the lid that happened when our youngest, Tommy, knocked it off the counter back in '84—he was just a boy then, always running through the house like a tornado. Anyway, she’ll reach for that butter dish and just start slathering it on the vegetables, or she'll scoop a great big mountain of mashed potatoes onto my plate and then drown it in gravy. \n\nAnd I sit there, looking at that full plate, and I just... I get this terrible knot in my stomach. I get so nervous, doctor. I really do. I look at all that heavy food, all that butter, and I just think, if I eat this, if I go back to eating the way she wants me to, I'm going to put all that weight right back on. I'll lose all the progress I've made, all the control I've worked so hard to keep. I'll be back to having aching knees and huffing and puffing just to pull a few weeds by the tomatoes. It just makes me so anxious, seeing her pile the food up like that. I have to be careful, you see, or it’ll all just slip right away from me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about eating or when you're faced with food?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, exactly, doctor, that's just what I was getting at a moment ago. When I sit down at our dining table—it's a beautiful heavy oak table, I actually refinished the whole thing myself back in '98, took me three solid weeks of sanding out in the garage just to get the old varnish off—and I see Martha coming through the swinging door with those serving bowls... well, my heart just starts to flutter. It really does. \n\nLike I was saying, when she tries to put butter on every little thing, or when she sets down a plate in front of me that's just piled high to the ceiling, I get so terribly nervous. My palms actually get a little clammy. I just stare at all that heavy food and I think, if I give in and eat this, I'm going to start putting all that weight right back on. I'll just balloon right back up and undo everything. I've worked so very, very hard to get this... this discipline, you know? This control over my body and my portions. \n\nAnd the thought of losing that control just because she wants me to finish a giant helping of her green bean casserole—the one with the fried onions on top, you know, the recipe from the back of the mushroom soup can—it just fills me with dread. It feels like if I take even one normal-sized bite of something that rich, the floodgates will open and I'll lose my grip on everything I've achieved. So, yes, anxious is absolutely the right word for it. I just sit there and worry the whole time she's dishing it out.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would be afraid of gaining weight if you were to eat more?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose I sound like a broken record, don't I? But yes, afraid is a very good word for it. Terrified, even, sometimes. It's exactly like I was just saying about Martha and her cooking. When she comes at me with that butter knife, or when she slides a plate across the table that looks like it's meant for a lumberjack instead of an old man whose biggest exertion is walking down to the mailbox... I just freeze up. \n\nI look at that food and I think, if I start eating more, if I eat the way she wants me to, it's just going to stick right to my ribs. I'll start putting the weight back on, pound by pound. And it's not just about the numbers on the scale, doctor, though I do check that every morning—first thing, right after I shave, before I even put my socks on. It's about the control. I have worked so incredibly hard to get this routine down, to know exactly what I'm putting into my body. \n\nIf I let myself eat more, if I just give in and have a second helping or let her butter my toast, I feel like all that control will just vanish into thin air. I'll be right back where I started, feeling heavy and sluggish, and all this effort, all this discipline I've built up day after day, week after week... it'll all be for nothing. So yes, the fear of gaining it all back is always right there, sitting on my shoulder at every single meal.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like eating less is a way for you to maintain control over your life?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose it is about control, in a manner of speaking. It's funny you put it that way, because... well, I was just telling you about Martha, wasn't I? It all comes back to the kitchen, it seems. We've had that same linoleum floor in the kitchen since 1974, you know—harvest gold, they called the color back then, with little flecks of brown in it. I remember laying it down myself, on a weekend in October. \n\nBut anyway, when I'm standing on that floor, and she's trying to slip a pat of butter onto my vegetables, or when she sets down a plate that's just brimming from edge to edge... that's when I feel it the most. That nervousness I mentioned. It's like a tightening right here in my chest. Because if I eat that full plate, if I let her butter my food the way she used to before I started being careful... well, I just know I'll start putting the weight back on. \n\nAnd if the weight comes back, then what do I have left? I'll have lost all that control I've worked so diligently to maintain. I mean, it's not easy, doctor, keeping this routine. It takes a certain kind of focus to say no to a slice of Martha's cherry pie—she uses tart cherries, the kind that make your mouth pucker just a little, and a lattice crust that she weaves by hand. But I have to say no, because eating less, keeping those portions small and exact... it's the only way I know I won't lose my grip on everything and go right back to being heavy. So yes, keeping the food down is how I keep from losing the control I've fought so hard for.\n\nDoctor: Is your decision to eat less mostly because you are afraid of gaining weight or because you want to feel in control of your body?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I feel like we're walking around the same tree here, don't you? Because to me, they aren't really two different things at all. They're tied together like a knot you just can't undo. \n\nYou see, like I've been saying, when Martha—bless her heart, she means well, she really does, we've been married fifty-two years this coming August—but when she tries to slip that extra butter onto my peas, or when she serves me one of those full plates that just covers every square inch of the china... it's the Royal Doulton china, by the way, the set with the little blue cornflowers on the rim. We used to only bring it out for Thanksgiving or Easter, but lately she uses it on a random Tuesday just to try and make the meal look more appealing, hoping I'll eat more. \n\nAnyway, when I see that overflowing plate, the nervousness hits me right away. It's the fear, absolutely. I get so terribly nervous that if I give in and eat all of that, I'll start putting the weight right back on. And if I put the weight back on, well, then I've lost the control I've worked so incredibly hard to keep. So, I suppose it's the fear of the weight coming back that really drives it, because gaining the weight means I've lost my grip on the control. It's all just one and the same to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would look better or feel better about yourself if you weighed more?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I certainly wouldn't look better, and I definitely wouldn't feel better about myself if I weighed more. In fact, it's quite the opposite, doctor. \n\nIt's all about how I feel in my clothes, you see. I wear these trousers—khakis, mostly, the kind with the flat front. I've bought the same brand from a catalog for years, since they stopped carrying them at the department store downtown. And I have this brown leather belt. It's worn in, soft as butter now, with a brass buckle that's lost a bit of its shine. If I put those trousers on in the morning and my belt feels a notch looser, well... If I'm standing there in the bathroom—the mirror is right above the sink, gets all fogged up from the hot water when I shave, so I have to wipe it down with a towel—if I look in that mirror and my stomach looks the least bit rounded... even just a fraction of an inch... it just ruins me. I feel so incredibly sloppy. I look at myself and I feel this deep, deep disappointment wash over me. I think, 'You let yourself go, you old fool.' I feel heavy and out of sorts, and it's all I can think about while I'm sitting there trying to read the morning news. \n\nSo, no, gaining weight wouldn't make me feel better at all. The very idea of it just brings up that awful, sloppy feeling. I have to keep the stomach flat, keep that belt on the tighter notch, or else I just can't feel good about myself when I look in that mirror.\n\nDoctor: Is your main goal in limiting your food intake to avoid gaining weight or to feel more in control of your life?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it seems like we're just going round and round the same bush, doesn't it? I know you doctors have your clipboards and your specific questions you have to check off, but like I was trying to explain just a moment ago... it's really not an either-or kind of situation for me. \n\nIt's... well, let's go back to Martha and the butter. We buy the unsalted kind, you know, in those little quarter-pound sticks wrapped in wax paper. She keeps it in a ceramic butter dish on the counter so it's always soft. And when I see her reaching for that dish, taking that butter knife—the one with the little pearl handle that belonged to her mother—and she's about to slide a pat of it onto my green beans or my carrots... or when she sets down one of those plates that's just piled high, edge to edge... that's when the nervousness really flares up in me. \n\nMy main goal, if you want to call it a goal, is just to stop that feeling. Because the moment I see that butter, or that full plate, the fear just grips me. I get so incredibly nervous that if I eat it, if I let her feed me the way she wants to, I'm going to start putting the weight right back on. And if that weight comes back, well, then all this effort, all this discipline... it's gone. I'll have lost all the control I've worked so very hard to keep. So, you see, the fear of gaining the weight and the fear of losing the control... they're the exact same thing when I'm sitting at that kitchen table. I just can't separate them for you.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your weight is lower than what is healthy for someone of your age and height?\n\nPatient: Well, honestly, I don't really see why everyone is making such a tremendous fuss about my weight. It just baffles me, doctor, it really does. Martha, my daughter Susan—who calls every Sunday evening right after dinner, like clockwork—and now you. \n\nYou know, when you get to be my age—I'll be seventy-nine next March, if you can believe it, born the same year the war ended—you're just not supposed to eat like a teenager anymore. Your metabolism slows down, your digestion gets finicky. I remember my own father, he lived to be eighty-six, and in his last decade, he practically lived on toast and tea. Nobody dragged him to a doctor to complain he was too thin. It’s just the natural order of things for older folks to eat less.\n\nAnd it's not as if I'm bedridden or wasting away, for heaven's sake. I'm still managing my chores just fine. Every morning, I'm out there in the yard. I rake the leaves off the front walk—we have this massive oak tree that just dumps leaves all autumn long, takes me a good forty-five minutes to get them all bagged up. I take the trash bins down to the curb on Thursdays. I even do my little tours around the neighborhood. I walk down to the corner store, past the old Henderson place, to pick up my newspaper. I've been doing that same walk for thirty years. My legs work fine, my wind is good. \n\nSo, no, I don't think my weight is lower than what's healthy. If I were truly unhealthy, I wouldn't be able to keep the yard looking neat or take my morning walks, would I? I think people just have these modern ideas about what an old man should look like, but I feel perfectly fine. I'm just living the way a man my age ought to live, keeping active and not overindulging. I really just don't understand the fuss.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would look better if you weighed less than you do now?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I know we already touched on this a bit when you asked if I'd look better if I weighed more, but... it's all tied together, really. You see, it's not so much about a specific number on the scale for me, or even just looking \"better\" in some general sense. I feel like I'm doing what I'm supposed to do, like I'm maintaining my standards. It's a very satisfying feeling, standing there in the bedroom with the morning light coming through the blinds, knowing I haven't let myself slip. \n\nBut if I were to weigh more, or even just stay the same when I know I could be doing better... it all comes back to that bathroom mirror. The one over the sink. If I stand there and I see even the slightest rounding of my stomach—even just a fraction—it completely ruins the picture. I just feel so terribly sloppy. I look at myself and think, 'Look at you, you're losing your grip.' It's a profound disappointment. It's not that I don't enjoy it. Goodness, my wife—she’s a wonderful cook, always has been. Why, just this past Sunday, she made her famous pot roast. She’s been making it the exact same way since we bought our first house over on Maple Drive, back in... oh, it must have been '71 or '72. She slow-cooks it all afternoon with the little pearl onions and the carrots, the ones I bring in from the garden, and the whole house just smells absolutely heavenly. My mouth still waters just smelling it, it really does. So my taste buds are working just fine, doctor, I can promise you that! \n\nI still love the taste of a good meal. I really do. It’s just that... well, I just don't need a great big heaping plate of it anymore. I'll take a little sliver of the meat, maybe a carrot or two, and I savor every single bite. I probably enjoy those few bites more now than I did when I was wolfing down food in my thirties before rushing back to work! But if I eat any more than that, it just... it feels so uncomfortable. It sits right here in my belly, like a rock, and makes me feel so sluggish. \n\nBut my wife, she sees me take a small portion and she takes it so personal. She thinks I don't like her cooking anymore! I keep telling her, 'Martha, it's the best roast in the county, I just don't have the room for a lumberjack's portion.' But she just sighs and shakes her head at me. She expects me to clear a massive plate like I used to. So, no, the food still tastes just as wonderful as it always did. I just enjoy a much smaller amount of it, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself forgetting to eat?\n\nPatient: Well, forgetting... no, I wouldn't say I forget. My memory is still as sharp as a tack, thank the Lord. I actually still do the crossword puzzle every single morning—in pen, mind you! So it's certainly not a memory issue. I always know exactly what time it is. We have this beautiful old grandfather clock out in the front hallway, the one Martha's parents gave us when they downsized back in the late eighties, and it chimes every hour on the hour. \n\nSo I'll hear it strike noon, and I know perfectly well it's lunchtime. I'll be sitting there in my armchair, maybe watching the midday local news with Jim Sanderson—he's been doing the broadcast for years now, good fellow—and I'll hear the chime. When I sit down at our dining table—it's a beautiful heavy oak table, I actually refinished the whole thing myself back in '98, took me three solid weeks of sanding out in the garage just to get the old varnish off—and I see Martha coming through the swinging door with those serving bowls... well, my heart just starts to flutter. I'll start putting the weight back on, pound by pound. I'll be right back where I started, feeling heavy and sluggish, and all this effort, all this discipline I've built up day after day, week after week... it'll all be for nothing. Doctor, I... honestly, I feel like we are just marching around the exact same tree we've been marching around since I sat down in this chair. I know I've said this to you three times already, but I suppose I'll try to explain it one more time, maybe frame it differently so you can understand what I'm getting at.

Let me take you back to the dining room, back to that heavy oak table I was telling you about. You remember I mentioned the plates, the big ceramic ones with the blue cornflowers? I get this terrible, gripping nervousness. It just washes right over me. My heart starts beating a little faster under my shirt. Because I look at that plate, and I know that if I give in, if I eat that butter, if I clear that plate like she wants me to, I am going to start putting the weight back on. 

And here is the crux of it, doctor, the part I really need you to hear: if I put that weight back on, I lose the control. The control I have worked so incredibly hard to keep, day in and day out. Getting up at 5:30, checking the belt, keeping myself disciplined... all of that effort, all of that order I've built into my life, it vanishes if the weight comes back. The fear of the weight *is* the fear of losing the control. I get nervous about the weight because it means the control is gone. I just can't say one is stronger than the other when they are the exact same feeling to me. I don't know how else to lay it out for you.

Why put gas in the car if it hasn't left the driveway, right?\n\nDoctor: Are you trying to lose weight?\n\nPatient: Well, trying to lose weight... I suppose it's more about not wanting to go backwards, you know? Like I said, I've gotten used to feeling lighter, feeling a bit more spry in the garden and on my walks. It took some doing to get to this point, to get this sort of... handle on things, I guess you could call it. \n\nThe trouble really starts when Martha gets going in the kitchen. Bless her heart, she grew up on a farm just outside of town, and she cooks like she's feeding a crew of threshers. She’s got this old blue ceramic butter dish, the one with the little chip on the lid that happened when our youngest, Tommy, knocked it off the counter back in '84—he was just a boy then, always running through the house like a tornado. Anyway, she’ll reach for that butter dish and just start slathering it on the vegetables, or she'll scoop a great big mountain of mashed potatoes onto my plate and then drown it in gravy. \n\nAnd I sit there, looking at that full plate, and I just... I get this terrible knot in my stomach. I get so nervous, doctor. I really do. I look at all that heavy food, all that butter, and I just think, if I eat this, if I go back to eating the way she wants me to, I'm going to put all that weight right back on. I'll lose all the progress I've made, all the control I've worked so hard to keep. I'll be back to having aching knees and huffing and puffing just to pull a few weeds by the tomatoes. It just makes me so anxious, seeing her pile the food up like that. I have to be careful, you see, or it’ll all just slip right away from me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about eating or when you're faced with food?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, exactly, doctor, that's just what I was getting at a moment ago. When I sit down at our dining table—it's a beautiful heavy oak table, I actually refinished the whole thing myself back in '98, took me three solid weeks of sanding out in the garage just to get the old varnish off—and I see Martha coming through the swinging door with those serving bowls... well, my heart just starts to flutter. It really does. \n\nLike I was saying, when she tries to put butter on every little thing, or when she sets down a plate in front of me that's just piled high to the ceiling, I get so terribly nervous. I'll just balloon right back up and undo everything. I've worked so very, very hard to get this... this discipline, you know? Doctor, I... I am honestly starting to wonder if this is some sort of test. Are you testing my memory? Or my patience? Because I am sitting here, looking at you, and I am just flabbergasted. I truly am. We have been over this, and over this, and over this again. I’ve been trying to tell you about how things are at home, especially around dinnertime. Because I know—I know with absolute certainty—that if I give in and eat what she’s trying to serve me, if I eat that butter or clear that full plate, I am going to start putting the weight back on. 

And, doctor, this is the part I keep trying to hammer home: if I put that weight back on, I lose the control. All of it. The discipline I’ve maintained, the careful order I’ve built into my life to keep things manageable... it all goes out the window if the weight comes back. The fear of gaining the weight is exactly the same thing as the need to feel in control of my body. They are one and the same. I restrict what I eat because gaining weight means losing the control I have worked so incredibly hard to keep. 

Please, doctor, I’ve explained this five times now. Can we please, finally, move on to a different question?

I'll be sitting there in my armchair, maybe watching the midday local news with Jim Sanderson—he's been doing the broadcast for years now, good fellow—and I'll hear the chime. But I just sit there and think about it, and I realize I just had my coffee and toast a few hours prior, and my stomach is perfectly quiet. I'm simply not hungry. So I don't forget to eat, I just... well, I make a conscious decision to skip it because my body isn't asking for anything. \n\nAnd honestly, even if I did happen to lose track of time, which I really don't, Martha is always right there anyway. She'll come bustling into the living room, wiping her hands on her kitchen towel, fussing that it's past one o'clock and I haven't had a bite. So there's absolutely no chance of forgetting with her around, but even on my own, it's really just a matter of not needing it, rather than it slipping my mind. It's just that... well, when you get to be seventy-eight years old, you just aren't out there burning the energy like a young man anymore. Big, heavy meals just feel completely unnecessary at my age. They just sit in your stomach like a lead weight, you know? You just don't need all that food when you're mostly sitting around the house. But try telling her that! She thinks I need to be eating three square meals a day like I'm still doing hard labor, and I keep trying to explain to her that my body just doesn't require all that...\n\nDoctor: Have you lost any weight recently?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, it's funny you should ask about the weight, because my regular doctor, Dr. Henderson—I've been seeing him for, oh, must be fifteen years now, ever since Dr. Miller retired—he was just saying the other day that the number on the scale has gotten a bit too low for his liking. He had me step on that old mechanical scale they have in the hallway, the one with the little sliding weights, and he made this sort of 'hmm' sound. He said I've dropped a fair bit since my last checkup. \n\nBut honestly, I just don't see what all the fuss is about. I was trying to explain to him, and I tell my wife this all the time, being a bit lighter on my feet is actually a blessing at my age! You see, I have this garden out back—mostly tomatoes and some squash, nothing too fancy, but it takes work to keep the weeds at bay—and carrying around less weight just makes it so much easier to get down in the dirt and tend to things. And my daily walks! I take a stroll down to the corner store and back every morning, rain or shine, and I tell you, my knees don't ache nearly as much as they used to when I was heavier. It just makes sense, doesn't it? Less weight to carry means less strain on the old joints. So, yes, the scale might be down a bit, but as far as I'm concerned, it's just making it easier for me to get around and enjoy my day. I feel spry! But try getting them to see it that way... they just look at the numbers.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself enjoying food less often than you used to?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, not at all. It's not that I don't enjoy it. Goodness, my wife—she’s a wonderful cook, always has been. Why, just this past Sunday, she made her famous pot roast. She’s been making it the exact same way since we bought our first house over on Maple Drive, back in... oh, it must have been '71 or '72. She slow-cooks it all afternoon with the little pearl onions and the carrots, the ones I bring in from the garden, and the whole house just smells absolutely heavenly. My mouth still waters just smelling it, it really does. So my taste buds are working just fine, doctor, I can promise you that! \n\nI still love the taste of a good meal. I really do. It’s just that... well, I just don't need a great big heaping plate of it anymore. I'll take a little sliver of the meat, maybe a carrot or two, and I savor every single bite. I probably enjoy those few bites more now than I did when I was wolfing down food in my thirties before rushing back to work! But if I eat any more than that, it just... it feels so uncomfortable. It sits right here in my belly, like a rock, and makes me feel so sluggish. \n\nBut my wife, she sees me take a small portion and she takes it so personal. She thinks I don't like her cooking anymore! I keep telling her, 'Martha, it's the best roast in the county, I just don't have the room for a lumberjack's portion.' But she just sighs and shakes her head at me. She expects me to clear a massive plate like I used to. So, no, the food still tastes just as wonderful as it always did. I just enjoy a much smaller amount of it, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself forgetting to eat?\n\nPatient: Well, forgetting... no, I wouldn't say I forget. My memory is still as sharp as a tack, thank the Lord. I actually still do the crossword puzzle every single morning—in pen, mind you! So it's certainly not a memory issue. I always know exactly what time it is. We have this beautiful old grandfather clock out in the front hallway, the one Martha's parents gave us when they downsized back in the late eighties, and it chimes every hour on the hour. \n\nSo I'll hear it strike noon, and I know perfectly well it's lunchtime. I'll be sitting there in my armchair, maybe watching the midday local news with Jim Sanderson—he's been doing the broadcast for years now, good fellow—and I'll hear the chime. But I just sit there and think about it, and I realize I just had my coffee and toast a few hours prior, and my stomach is perfectly quiet. I'm simply not hungry. So I don't forget to eat, I just... well, I make a conscious decision to skip it because my body isn't asking for anything. \n\nAnd honestly, even if I did happen to lose track of time, which I really don't, Martha is always right there anyway. She'll come bustling into the living room, wiping her hands on her kitchen towel, fussing that it's past one o'clock and I haven't had a bite. So there's absolutely no chance of forgetting with her around, but even on my own, it's really just a matter of not needing it, rather than it slipping my mind. Why put gas in the car if it hasn't left the driveway, right?\n\nDoctor: Are you trying to lose weight?\n\nPatient: Well, trying to lose weight... I suppose it's more about not wanting to go backwards, you know? Like I said, I've gotten used to feeling lighter, feeling a bit more spry in the garden and on my walks. It took some doing to get to this point, to get this sort of... handle on things, I guess you could call it. \n\nThe trouble really starts when Martha gets going in the kitchen. Bless her heart, she grew up on a farm just outside of town, and she cooks like she's feeding a crew of threshers. She’s got this old blue ceramic butter dish, the one with the little chip on the lid that happened when our youngest, Tommy, knocked it off the counter back in '84—he was just a boy then, always running through the house like a tornado. Anyway, she’ll reach for that butter dish and just start slathering it on the vegetables, or she'll scoop a great big mountain of mashed potatoes onto my plate and then drown it in gravy. \n\nAnd I sit there, looking at that full plate, and I just... I get this terrible knot in my stomach. I get so nervous, doctor. I really do. I look at all that heavy food, all that butter, and I just think, if I eat this, if I go back to eating the way she wants me to, I'm going to put all that weight right back on. I'll lose all the progress I've made, all the control I've worked so hard to keep. I'll be back to having aching knees and huffing and puffing just to pull a few weeds by the tomatoes. It just makes me so anxious, seeing her pile the food up like that. I have to be careful, you see, or it’ll all just slip right away from me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about eating or when you're faced with food?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, exactly, doctor, that's just what I was getting at a moment ago. When I sit down at our dining table—it's a beautiful heavy oak table, I actually refinished the whole thing myself back in '98, took me three solid weeks of sanding out in the garage just to get the old varnish off—and I see Martha coming through the swinging door with those serving bowls... well, my heart just starts to flutter. It really does. \n\nLike I was saying, when she tries to put butter on every little thing, or when she sets down a plate in front of me that's just piled high to the ceiling, I get so terribly nervous. My palms actually get a little clammy. I just stare at all that heavy food and I think, if I give in and eat this, I'm going to start putting all that weight right back on. I'll just balloon right back up and undo everything. I've worked so very, very hard to get this... this discipline, you know? This control over my body and my portions. \n\nAnd the thought of losing that control just because she wants me to finish a giant helping of her green bean casserole—the one with the fried onions on top, you know, the recipe from the back of the mushroom soup can—it just fills me with dread. It feels like if I take even one normal-sized bite of something that rich, the floodgates will open and I'll lose my grip on everything I've achieved. So, yes, anxious is absolutely the right word for it. I just sit there and worry the whole time she's dishing it out.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would be afraid of gaining weight if you were to eat more?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose I sound like a broken record, don't I? But yes, afraid is a very good word for it. Terrified, even, sometimes. It's exactly like I was just saying about Martha and her cooking. When she comes at me with that butter knife, or when she slides a plate across the table that looks like it's meant for a lumberjack instead of an old man whose biggest exertion is walking down to the mailbox... I just freeze up. \n\nI look at that food and I think, if I start eating more, if I eat the way she wants me to, it's just going to stick right to my ribs. I'll start putting the weight back on, pound by pound. And it's not just about the numbers on the scale, doctor, though I do check that every morning—first thing, right after I shave, before I even put my socks on. It's about the control. I have worked so incredibly hard to get this routine down, to know exactly what I'm putting into my body. \n\nIf I let myself eat more, if I just give in and have a second helping or let her butter my toast, I feel like all that control will just vanish into thin air. I'll be right back where I started, feeling heavy and sluggish, and all this effort, all this discipline I've built up day after day, week after week... it'll all be for nothing. So yes, the fear of gaining it all back is always right there, sitting on my shoulder at every single meal.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like eating less is a way for you to maintain control over your life?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose it is about control, in a manner of speaking. It's funny you put it that way, because... well, I was just telling you about Martha, wasn't I? It all comes back to the kitchen, it seems. We've had that same linoleum floor in the kitchen since 1974, you know—harvest gold, they called the color back then, with little flecks of brown in it. I remember laying it down myself, on a weekend in October. \n\nBut anyway, when I'm standing on that floor, and she's trying to slip a pat of butter onto my vegetables, or when she sets down a plate that's just brimming from edge to edge... that's when I feel it the most. That nervousness I mentioned. It's like a tightening right here in my chest. Because if I eat that full plate, if I let her butter my food the way she used to before I started being careful... well, I just know I'll start putting the weight back on. \n\nAnd if the weight comes back, then what do I have left? I'll have lost all that control I've worked so diligently to maintain. I mean, it's not easy, doctor, keeping this routine. It takes a certain kind of focus to say no to a slice of Martha's cherry pie—she uses tart cherries, the kind that make your mouth pucker just a little, and a lattice crust that she weaves by hand. But I have to say no, because eating less, keeping those portions small and exact... it's the only way I know I won't lose my grip on everything and go right back to being heavy. So yes, keeping the food down is how I keep from losing the control I've fought so hard for.\n\nDoctor: Is your decision to eat less mostly because you are afraid of gaining weight or because you want to feel in control of your body?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I feel like we're walking around the same tree here, don't you? Because to me, they aren't really two different things at all. They're tied together like a knot you just can't undo. \n\nYou see, like I've been saying, when Martha—bless her heart, she means well, she really does, we've been married fifty-two years this coming August—but when she tries to slip that extra butter onto my peas, or when she serves me one of those full plates that just covers every square inch of the china... it's the Royal Doulton china, by the way, the set with the little blue cornflowers on the rim. It's the fear, absolutely. I get so terribly nervous that if I give in and eat all of that, I'll start putting the weight right back on. And if I put the weight back on, well, then I've lost the control I've worked so incredibly hard to keep. So, I suppose it's the fear of the weight coming back that really drives it, because gaining the weight means I've lost my grip on the control. It's all just one and the same to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would look better or feel better about yourself if you weighed more?\n\nPatient: Well, no... no, I certainly wouldn't look better, and I definitely wouldn't feel better about myself if I weighed more. In fact, it's quite the opposite, doctor. \n\nIt's all about how I feel in my clothes, you see. I wear these trousers—khakis, mostly, the kind with the flat front. I've bought the same brand from a catalog for years, since they stopped carrying them at the department store downtown. And I have this brown leather belt. It's worn in, soft as butter now, with a brass buckle that's lost a bit of its shine. If I put those trousers on in the morning and my belt feels a notch looser, well... I'll go out and get the paper feeling sharp, feeling put together.\n\nBut if it goes the other way... oh, that's a completely different story. If I'm standing there in the bathroom—the mirror is right above the sink, gets all fogged up from the hot water when I shave, so I have to wipe it down with a towel—if I look in that mirror and my stomach looks the least bit rounded... even just a fraction of an inch... it just ruins me. I feel so incredibly sloppy. I look at myself and I feel this deep, deep disappointment wash over me. I think, 'You let yourself go, you old fool.' The very idea of it just brings up that awful, sloppy feeling. I have to keep the stomach flat, keep that belt on the tighter notch, or else I just can't feel good about myself when I look in that mirror.\n\nDoctor: Is your main goal in limiting your food intake to avoid gaining weight or to feel more in control of your life?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it seems like we're just going round and round the same bush, doesn't it? And she’ll try to put butter on my vegetables, or she’ll set down one of those big, heavy ceramic plates with the blue cornflowers on it, and it will just be piled high. I mean, completely full, edge to edge, with food. \n\nAnd when she does that, when I see that full plate or that butter, I don't just feel a little uneasy. I get this overwhelming, terrible nervousness. It just grips me right in the chest. Because I know—I know with absolute certainty—that if I give in and eat what she’s trying to serve me, if I eat that butter or clear that full plate, I am going to start putting the weight back on. \n\nAnd, doctor, this is the part I keep trying to hammer home: if I put that weight back on, I lose the control. All of it. The discipline I’ve maintained, the careful order I’ve built into my life to keep things manageable... it all goes out the window if the weight comes back. The fear of gaining the weight is exactly the same thing as the need to feel in control of my body. They are one and the same. I restrict what I eat because gaining weight means losing the control I have worked so incredibly hard to keep. \n\nPlease, doctor, I’ve explained this five times now. Can we please, finally, move on to a different question?"
